types.blurb_en: The founding house type of TMR. When Frederick Todd laid out the town in 1912 he was borrowing directly from Ebenezer Howard's Garden City movement, and the first houses near the station borrowed the movement's architecture too: the English Arts-and-Crafts cottage of Letchworth and Hampstead Garden Suburb. Look for steep 45° gables, a brick ground floor with stucco or half-timbering above, small-paned windows, and a deliberately picturesque, asymmetrical silhouette that reads as a cottage in a garden rather than a house on a street.
types.origin_en: The Garden City movement's architecture as well as its planning. Ebenezer Howard's 1898 tract produced Letchworth (Parker & Unwin, 1903) and Hampstead Garden Suburb (1907), and their house vocabulary, itself drawn from Voysey, Baillie Scott and the English cottage, travelled with the idea: steep gables, roughcast or half-timbered upper storeys over brick, small-paned casements, picturesque asymmetry, the house read as a cottage in a garden. The by-law's Garden City House is this, with the 45° roof, stucco-and-timber upper floor and small brick module written out as criteria.

types.blurb_en: “Faubourien” refers to the vernacular of Montreal's old inner suburbs (the faubourgs): a plain two-storey brick box, flat or hipped roof, sometimes a false mansard, and a front verandah on wooden columns. In TMR the type is what the Plateau or Rosemont row house becomes when it is given its own lot, a side driveway and a lawn. Its virtue is restraint: symmetry, aligned windows, one material.
types.origin_en: Faubourien points to the maison de faubourg, the plain brick house of Québec's nineteenth-century inner suburbs: two or three storeys, flat or false-mansard roof, aligned openings, minimal ornament, a front gallery on wooden posts. Montreal's Plateau PIIA uses the same term for its own housing stock. In TMR the type is what that urban house becomes on a detached or semi-detached lot with a side driveway; several examples take on the cubic mass and hipped roof of the American Foursquare, which was being built across Canada in the same years.

types.blurb_en: The interwar Montreal walk-up, three storeys of red brick under a flat roof, with a decorated parapet, a stone base, patterned brickwork and a prominent entrance portico. Balconies with iron or stone railings give the façade its rhythm. These sit on the town's few multi-family lots and are the collective sibling of the faubourg house.
types.origin_en: Three-storey brick apartment houses of the 1920s and 30s, Montreal's standard multi-family building of the period. This is where Art Deco actually lives in TMR: stepped and decorated parapets, geometric brick panels, artificial-stone entrance surrounds, iron balcony rails with angular motifs. Héritage Montréal describes the same repertoire on 1920s Montreal plexes (dark brick, artificial-stone insertions around doors and windows, appliqués with geometric forms). The by-law absorbs it as "distinctive brick motifs and bonds" and "a body crowned by a brick motif and a parapet" rather than naming the style.

types.blurb_en: A 1930s–50s revival of the 18th-century Quebec farmhouse: a steep roof whose eaves flare out into “larmiers” that shelter the front door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, and a calm symmetrical front. It was the domestic face of a broader interwar interest in Québécois heritage. The distinctive move is the roof, which is asked to express the base of the house through its overhang.
types.origin_en: A regionalist revival of the eighteenth-century Laurentian farmhouse: bell-cast roof whose eaves flare into larmiers sheltering the door, a row of dormers, fieldstone walls, a calm symmetrical front. The Canadian Encyclopedia locates its source in the anglophone rediscovery of pre-industrial Québec during the 1920s–30s, stimulated by Clarence Gagnon's paintings and encouraged by Percy Nobbs and Ramsay Traquair at McGill, whose surveys of old Québec buildings fed a fashion for fieldstone and pitched roofs among the province's leading domestic architects. TMR's Canadian houses are the suburban, builder-scale version of that fashion.

types.blurb_en: Colonial Revival as it arrived from the American Northeast: a long, simple gabled rectangle with its broad side to the street, symmetrical windows, dormers set halfway up the roof, and a discreet canopy over the front door. Brick or stone below, clapboard or stucco above. It is quieter than the Georgian house, and the by-law wants it kept quiet: bay windows are the only projections allowed.
types.origin_en: A long side-gabled rectangle with its broad face to the street, symmetrical openings, dormers half-way up the roof, a discreet door canopy; brick or stone below and clapboard or stucco above. It is the New England colonial house as codified in 1920s–40s pattern books and builders' plan services, the quieter cousin of Georgian Revival. The by-law keeps it quiet: bay windows are the only projections it allows.

types.blurb_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment courts arranged in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. A stone base and stone string courses tie them to the collegiate-Tudor mood of the interwar decades. Entrances are marked by a distinct architectural element rather than a big portico.
types.origin_en: Low-rise red-brick apartment blocks in U or L plans around a green forecourt, with stone bases, stone string courses, steep gables, dormers and the occasional turret. The idiom is the residential cousin of interwar school and college architecture, and of the "garden apartment" courts built across North America in the 1930s–40s. The by-law's "New England (collective)" label is looser than the architecture: these blocks are more Tudor than New England.

types.blurb_en: Georgian Revival: the most formal of TMR's houses. A red-brick box of two full storeys, three or five bays wide, with a central door flanked by pilasters and topped by an elaborate crown, sash windows with small panes, and a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gabled roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law lets you emphasise the central bay with a slight projection and a pediment, and nothing more.
types.origin_en: The formal wing of Colonial Revival. Two full storeys of red brick, three or five bays, a central door with pilasters and an entablature or pediment, sash windows with small panes, a frieze under a moderately pitched hip or side-gable roof. Symmetry is the whole point; the by-law permits one flourish, a slightly projected central bay under a pediment, and nothing else. In Canada the style carried an Imperial-loyalist inflection that made it a natural fit for a town founded and first settled by anglophones.

types.blurb_en: Tudor Revival, TMR's most romantic type: steep 45° roofs broken into several gables, a natural-stone ground floor with brick or half-timbered stucco above, patterned brickwork (herringbone, Dutch bond), small-paned casements, sometimes a round turret at the entrance. Where the Georgian house is symmetrical, the manor is deliberately picturesque, and its garage is meant to hide.
types.origin_en: The by-law's "English manor" is Tudor Revival by any other name: stone ground floor with brick or stucco-and-timber above, patterned brick (herringbone, Dutch bond), 45° multi-gabled roofs, small-paned casements, sometimes a round entrance turret. In North America the style peaked in the 1920s–30s and lingered into the 1940s; its Montreal fashion was strongest in the anglophone west end and suburbs. Tudor detailing also surfaces on some Phase 1 Garden City houses, which is why the two types share the half-timbered gable.

types.blurb_en: The postwar ranch bungalow: one storey, long and low, with a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, and big undivided windows wider than they are tall. Buff (“chamois”) brick or stone, black shingles, a wide driveway. The type that arrived with the car and the last empty lots of the 1950s and 60s.
types.origin_en: One storey, long and low, a shallow-pitched roof whose overhang shelters a recessed door, a garage pushed forward into the façade, big undivided windows wider than tall, buff ("chamois") brick or stone, a wide driveway. In Québec usage bungalow simply means the postwar single-family suburban house; the form is the Ranch house that spread from the American Southwest after 1945 and became the default Canadian suburban dwelling of the 1950s–60s.

types.blurb_en: In Quebec usage a “cottage” is simply a two-storey detached house, and this is its postwar version: a plain box under a low hip roof, stone or brick on the ground floor with stucco or siding above, garage built into the front, and a flat marquise over the door. A visible line at the ground-floor lintels or the upper sills divides base from body.
types.origin_en: In Québec real-estate usage a cottage is a two-storey detached house, as opposed to the one-storey bungalow; the OQLF notes the word's British origin and its earlier sense of an elegant, English-inspired country house. TMR's postwar cottage is a plain box: stone or brick base, stucco or siding above, low hip roof, integrated garage, flat marquise over the door, a horizontal line at the ground-floor lintels or upper sills dividing base from body. Some examples keep vestigial colonial detailing (Minimal Traditional); others, in cut stone with flat roofs and rounded or banded corners, are the town's clearest echo of Streamline Moderne.

types.blurb_en: Two volumes offset by half a storey: a one-storey wing beside a one-and-a-half-storey wing, with the garage tucked under the bedrooms and pushed forward, and a recessed entrance under the eaves. Salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels; both roofs share one low-pitched material. The interior stair does the work the façade shows.
types.origin_en: A plan type more than a style, dominant across North American suburbs from the mid-1950s: two volumes offset by half a storey, the garage under the bedrooms and pushed forward, a recessed entrance under the eaves. TMR's are dressed in Ranch and Contemporary materials, salmon, buff or brown stone with wood or metal infill panels, under one shared low-pitched roof.

types.blurb_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom, filtered through 1960s Montreal: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked right under the eaves and running around the corners as ribbons, long “Roman” brick or long-cut stone, and one-storey wings (garage, porch, solarium) that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical, and the most architect-driven of the phase-3 types.
types.origin_en: Frank Lloyd Wright's Prairie idiom of 1900–1915, revived and simplified in the 1950s–60s Contemporary house: relentless horizontality, low pyramidal or multi-hipped roofs with deep soffits, upper windows tucked under the eaves and wrapping the corners as ribbons, long "Roman" brick or long-cut stone, one-storey wings that stretch the composition sideways. Asymmetrical and the most architect-driven of the Phase 3 types; the by-law's insistence on the Roman brick module is the tell.

types.blurb_en: The 1950s–70s modernist apartment building: flat roof finished with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor on top, balconies grouped into recessed loggias, wide undivided windows and a marquise over the door. Sand or red brick, often several brick colours on one façade. Parking goes underground; the front yard stays almost entirely green.
types.origin_en: Flat-roofed brick slabs of the 1950s–70s with a horizontal coping band, a set-back penthouse floor, loggia balconies and wide undivided windows, in sand or red brick and often several brick colours on one façade. The town's share of the postwar Modernism that lines Côte-des-Neiges and Sherbrooke; the earliest examples, with brick-and-stone banding, still carry a Streamline accent.
